idea.text: Indicators are dyes that change colour depending on whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline. Universal indicator shows a whole rainbow of colours across the pH scale from 1 to 14; litmus just turns red in acid and blue in alkali.
idea.analogy: Like a mood ring for liquids: the colour tells you how acidic or alkaline a solution is.

steps.title: 2 mL acid into tube 1
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL of dilute acid into tube 1. Small volumes: tilt gently.

whatIf.rate: A fast pour into a narrow test tube splashes. 2 mL is a small amount: tilt gently.
whatIf.overshoot: More liquid dilutes the indicator, so the colour comes out paler and harder to judge.
whatIf.quantity: A very different volume in each tube makes the colours harder to compare fairly.

explore.if: use 1 M acid instead of 0.1 M
explore.then: Still red: universal indicator shows pH, and both are very acidic (about pH 0 and pH 1). The difference is too small to see.

steps.title: 2 mL water into tube 2
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL of distilled water into tube 2.

whatIf.rate: A fast pour into a narrow test tube splashes. 2 mL is a small amount: tilt gently.
whatIf.overshoot: More liquid dilutes the indicator, so the colour comes out paler and harder to judge.
whatIf.quantity: A very different volume in each tube makes the colours harder to compare fairly.

explore.if: use tap water instead of distilled water
explore.then: Tap water has dissolved minerals and gases, so it might show yellow-green or blue-green instead of pure green.

steps.title: 2 mL alkali into tube 3
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL of dilute alkali into tube 3.

whatIf.rate: A fast pour into a narrow test tube splashes. 2 mL is a small amount: tilt gently.
whatIf.overshoot: More liquid dilutes the indicator, so the colour comes out paler and harder to judge.
whatIf.quantity: A very different volume in each tube makes the colours harder to compare fairly.

explore.if: use a weak alkali like baking soda solution
explore.then: Blue rather than purple: weak alkalis have a lower pH, around 8 to 9.

steps.title: Universal indicator: tube 1
steps.instruction: Add 2 drops of universal indicator to tube 1.

whatIf.order: Chemically it would still work, but put the liquid in first so you can watch the colour change as the drops land.
whatIf.not-dropwise: Pouring indicator floods the tube and makes the colour very dark. Two drops are enough to see it clearly.
whatIf.overshoot: Too many drops make the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.
whatIf.quantity: Too much indicator makes the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.

explore.if: add the indicator before the acid
explore.then: You'd get the same colour in the end: it depends on the final mixture, not on the order.

whatIf.order: Chemically it would still work, but put the water in first so you can watch the colour as the drops land.
whatIf.overshoot: Too many drops make the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.
whatIf.quantity: Too much indicator makes the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.

whatIf.order: Chemically it would still work, but put the alkali in first so you can watch the colour as the drops land.
whatIf.overshoot: Too many drops make the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.
whatIf.quantity: Too much indicator makes the colour very dark, so it's harder to judge which shade it is.

steps.title: 2 mL acid into tube 4
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL acid into tube 4.

whatIf.overshoot: More acid dilutes the litmus, so the red is paler.
whatIf.quantity: A very different volume makes the colours harder to compare fairly.

steps.title: Litmus in acid
steps.instruction: Pour 2 mL acid into tube 4, then add 2 drops of litmus.

whatIf.order: Chemically it would still work, but put the acid in first so you can see the litmus change.

explore.if: add litmus to the water instead
explore.then: Purple: neutral litmus sits halfway between its red and blue forms.

steps.title: 2 mL alkali into tube 5
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL alkali into tube 5.

whatIf.overshoot: More alkali dilutes the litmus, so the blue is paler.
whatIf.quantity: A very different volume makes the colours harder to compare fairly.

steps.title: Litmus in alkali
steps.instruction: Add 2 drops of litmus to tube 5.

whatIf.order: Chemically it would still work, but put the alkali in first so you can see the litmus change.

explore.if: use litmus paper instead of litmus solution
explore.then: Same idea: red paper turns blue in alkali, blue paper turns red in acid. Paper is handy for a quick test.

vol-1.text: How much is 2 mL in a test tube? Look at the tube's height.

vol-2.text: Tilt the bottle just past the point where it starts to pour and watch the volume counter.

ind-1.text: Indicators are strong dyes. A little goes a long way.

ind-2.text: Tap the dropper bottle twice for 2 drops.

observations.whatHappened: Universal indicator turned red in the acid, green in water and blue-purple in the alkali. Litmus turned red in the acid and blue in the alkali.
observations.why: Indicators are weak acids whose two forms have different colours. Lots of H⁺ (acid) pushes them into one form; lots of OH⁻ (alkali) into the other. Universal indicator mixes several dyes, so it shows a whole rainbow across pH 1 to 14.
realWorld: Red cabbage as a kitchen indicator

prompts.question: What colour did universal indicator turn in distilled water?
prompts.explain: Pure water is neutral, pH 7, which is green on the universal indicator chart.

prompts.question: Litmus turned blue in tube 5. That tells you the liquid is...
prompts.explain: Litmus is blue in alkalis and red in acids.

captions.text: 2 mL each of acid, water and alkali into three tubes.
captions.why: Using the same small volume in each tube makes it a fair comparison.
captions.safety: These are dilute, but acid and alkali can still sting eyes and skin, so pour gently into the small tubes.

captions.text: Two drops of universal indicator in each...
captions.why: Universal indicator is a mix of several dyes. Each changes colour at a different pH, so together they make a rainbow.

captions.text: Red, green, purple: a pH rainbow. Now litmus in acid and alkali.
captions.why: Red means acidic (0.1 M hydrochloric acid is about pH 1), green means neutral (pH 7), purple means strongly alkaline (about pH 13). Litmus has only two colours: red in acid, blue in alkali.
